power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: BACKGROUND: Opioids prescribed for acute pain frequently remain unused, creating opportunities for unintended use, accidental ingestion, or diversion.
Little is known about counseling patients receive from prescribers or pharmacists on storage and disposal of opioids.
OBJECTIVE: To characterize clinician counseling on opioid disposal and patient-reported storage, use, and disposal practices among opioid-naïve patients prescribed opioids for acute pain.
DESIGN: Multicenter prospective cohort study with participant recruitment between September 2020 and March 2023.
PARTICIPANTS: Opioid-naïve patients prescribed opioids for acute pain in emergency departments, primary care or urgent care clinics, inpatient settings, and dental practices.

Patient-reported receipt of counseling on the importance of opioid disposal and appropriate disposal methods; opioid storage practices; use and disposition of prescribed opioids; disposal methods; and reasons for keeping or disposing of leftover opioids.
Among 1708 participants, the median age was 38 years (IQR, 28-52); most were recruited from emergency departments (n=915; 53.6%) and primary care or urgent care clinics (n=307; 18.0%).
Among 1233 participants who answered the question on counseling about the importance of opioid disposal, 811 (65.8%) reported receiving no counseling.
Among 1220 participants who answered the question on counseling about appropriate disposal methods, 832 (68.2%) reported receiving no counseling.
Among 812 participants who answered the question about storing opioids in a locked location, 610 (75.1%) reported never doing so.
Among 929 participants providing information on opioid leftovers and disposition, 618 (66.5%) did not use all prescribed opioids.
Among these 618 participants, 258 (42.8%) kept leftover opioids and 345 (57.2%) disposed of them.

Among 256 participants who reported reasons for keeping leftover opioids, 159 (62.1%) wanted medication available for the same condition, 70 (27.3%) wanted medication available for a different condition, and 36 (14.1%) did not know how to properly dispose of the medication.

CONCLUSIONS: Among opioid-naïve patients prescribed opioids for acute pain, counseling about opioid disposal was uncommon, secure storage was infrequent, and leftover opioids were frequent, with many patients keeping leftover opioids for possible future use.
These findings suggest opportunities to improve counseling on opioid storage and disposal and encourage safe disposal of unused opioids after acute pain treatment.

Opioid analgesics are frequently prescribed for the management of acute pain across diverse clinical settings. 1 Although opioids can provide effective pain relief when prescribed and used appropriately, their use is associated with serious harms, including adverse effects, tolerance, dependence, misuse, overdose, and death. [2] [3] [4] [5] Despite the dominant role of illicitly made synthetic opioids in overdose deaths, prescription opioid-related harms remain a major public health concern in the United States; in 2025, over 7,000 overdose deaths involved prescription opioids, 6 and 6.9 million people aged 12 years or older, including approximately 402,000 adolescents aged 12 to 17 years, reported misusing prescription opioids. 7 Among people who misused prescription pain relievers, many obtained them from friends or relatives, including receiving them for free, buying them, or taking them without asking, underscoring the importance of reducing unused prescription opioids in the home. 8, 9 Unused opioids after treatment for acute pain may contribute to the continued availability of prescription opioids in the home, where they may later be used without medical supervision, shared with or taken by others, or accidentally ingested.

text.text: Safe storage and timely disposal of unused opioids are therefore important strategies to reduce opioid availability in the home after acute pain treatment.

The US Food and Drug Administration recommends medication take-back programs, including mail-back envelopes, 14 as the preferred method for disposing of most unused medications, with flushing recommended for most opioid medicines when take-back options are not readily available. 15 Counseling by prescribers and pharmacists may help patients understand the importance of opioid disposal and appropriate disposal methods, 16 but evidence remains limited on counseling, storage, and disposal practices among patients prescribed opioids for acute pain across clinical settings.

text.text: The APP study (NCT04509115) was a multicenter prospective cohort study that enrolled opioid-naïve patients between September 2020 and March 2023 who were prescribed opioid analgesics for the management of acute pain across multiple clinical settings, including emergency departments, primary data collection methods for the APP study have been published previously. 17, 18 The study protocol was approved by the institutional review board at each participating site, and all participants provided written informed consent prior to enrollment.

text.text: This study was reported in accordance with the STROBE guidelines.

Eligible participants in the APP study included adults aged 18 years or older at all participating sites and adolescents aged 15 years or older undergoing impacted third molar extraction at the Mayo Clinic in Rochester, Minnesota.

Participants had acute pain of less than eight weeks' duration at the time of enrollment, reported no opioid use in the preceding six months, and were offered an outpatient prescription for an opioid analgesic for pain management, including participants discharged from inpatient hospitalizations with an opioid prescription.
Individuals with cancer-associated pain, end-of-life pain, or other pain conditions likely to progress to chronic pain were excluded, as were those who declined participation.
Participants completed baseline and follow-up surveys through the Hugo Health digital platform, accessible through personal smartphones or other internet-enabled devices.
Baseline surveys collected information on sociodemographic characteristics, clinical history, pain characteristics, treatments received, and social determinants of health.
Follow-up surveys captured daily pain intensity and opioid and nonopioid use, as well as weekly assessments of side effects and patient-reported outcomes.
Opioid storage practices were assessed through weekly surveys, using the first available weekly response for each participant.
When weekly survey data were unavailable, the end-of-study survey responses summarizing storage practices over the whole follow-up period were used.

Outcomes related to use of all prescribed opioids, keeping or disposing of leftover opioids, disposal methods, and reasons for keeping or disposing of leftover opioids were assessed through the survey administered 2 weeks after cessation of opioid use or the end-of-study survey; the last available response was used to capture the final disposition of opioid medications.
Receipt of counseling on the importance of opioid disposal and appropriate disposal methods was assessed through the week 1 survey, administered 1 week after enrollment.
Instructions received about when to start and stop taking opioids were assessed once at enrollment.
The counseling outcomes were patient-reported receipt of counseling on the importance of opioid disposal and receipt of counseling on appropriate disposal methods.
For each counseling outcome, participants reported whether counseling was received and whether it was provided only by a pharmacist, only by a prescriber, or by both a pharmacist and a prescriber.
Receipt of counseling was defined as reporting counseling by a pharmacist, prescriber, or both.

Among participants who reported receipt of counseling on appropriate disposal methods, we characterized the specific disposal methods recommended by the clinician, including return to a medication take-back location, flushing down the toilet, mixing with an undesirable substance, and use of a disposal kit.
Participants could report more than one recommended disposal method.
We also characterized patient-reported instructions on when to take and stop taking opioids.

Storage-related outcomes included patient-reported frequency of storing opioids in a latched location and in a locked location, each assessed using response options of never, almost never, sometimes, almost always, and always.

We also defined a composite storage outcome of storing opioids in a latched or locked location as reporting almost always or always for either storage in a latched location or storage in a locked location.
We characterized the type of storage container used, including original prescription bottle, daily or weekly pill organizer, single-compartment container, or other container.

Disposal-related outcomes included whether participants used all prescribed opioids, whether participants kept leftover opioids among those who did not use all prescribed opioids, and disposal methods used among participants who disposed of leftover opioids.
We also characterized patient-reported reasons for disposing of or keeping leftover opioids among participants who disposed of or kept them, respectively.
Participants could report more than one disposal method or reason.

Covariates included age group (≤21, 22-34, 35-44, 45-54, 55-64, and ≥65 years), presence of children in the household, race/ethnicity (Asian, American Indian or Alaska Native, Black or African American, Hispanic or Latino, Native Hawaiian or other Pacific Islander, White, other, or unknown), residential setting (urban, rural, or unknown), education level (less than high school, high school diploma or General Educational Development, more than high school, or unknown), clinical setting of care (emergency departments, primary care or urgent care clinics, inpatient settings, or dental practices), and pain source (dental, obstetric, surgical or procedural, trauma or injury, musculoskeletal, abdominal, renal colic/kidney stone, skin or soft tissue, low back pain, other, or unknown).
Data management and statistical analyses were performed using Stata version 18 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX, USA).
Categorical variables were summarized using counts and percentages, and continuous variables using medians and interquartile ranges (IQRs).
Survey response timing was summarized as the elapsed number of days from prescription offer to the survey response.
We used χ² tests to compare categorical outcomes across groups.
To estimate adjusted associations, we fit multivariable logistic regression models with robust standard errors and calculated risk ratios (RRs) as ratios of predictive margins.

Models for receipt of counseling on the importance of opioid disposal, receipt of counseling on appropriate disposal methods, and storing opioids in a latched or locked location included age group, clinical setting, pain source, and presence of children in the household.

The model for keeping leftover opioids was restricted to participants who did not use all prescribed opioids and included age group, clinical setting, and presence of children in the household; pain source was not included because of sparse cells and perfect prediction.

Due to missing data in the variable for whether people had leftover opioids, we used a multiple imputation analysis to assess the potential impact of this missing data; the analysis is described in the Supplement.
A 2-sided P value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.
This analysis was conducted as part of the larger APP study, which was not specifically designed to detect differences in opioid counseling, storage, and disposal outcomes across participant groups.
Therefore, these analyses were considered exploratory.

Among 1328 participants (77.8%) who provided information on instructions received about when to take opioids, 522 (39.3%) reported being instructed to take opioids only when pain was very bad, 317 (23.9%) at the first sign of pain, and 291 (21.9%) to try other medications before taking opioids.
Overall, 101 (7.6%) reported receiving no instructions on when to take opioids.

Among 1302 participants (76.2%) who provided information on instructions received about when to stop taking opioids, 417 (32.0%) reported being instructed to continue taking opioids as long as they had pain, 289 (22.2%) until the pills ran out, and 177 (13.6%) after a specified number of days.
Overall, 456 (35.0%) reported receiving no instructions on when to stop taking opioids.

Instructions differed across clinical settings, with participants recruited from inpatient settings most frequently reporting no instructions on when to take opioids (17.8%) and participants recruited from dental practices most frequently reporting instructions to continue taking opioids as long as pain persisted (41.5%) (Supplementary Table 2).

text.text: In this multicenter prospective cohort study of opioid-naïve patients prescribed opioids for acute pain, approximately two-thirds of respondents reported no counseling on the importance of opioid disposal or appropriate disposal methods, with counseling rates similar across clinical settings and pain sources.

Among participants who answered questions about locked storage, three-quarters reported never storing opioids in a locked location, although participants with children in the household were more likely to store opioids in a latched or locked location.

Approximately two-thirds of participants with information on opioid leftovers and disposition did not use all prescribed opioids, and more than 40% of those with leftover opioids kept them, most commonly because they wanted to have the medication available for possible future use.

Nearly 25% of those who disposed of leftover opioids did so in the trash, which is not recommended method for opioid disposal; instead, FDA recommends disposing of most opioids by flushing them down the toilet when take-back options or mail-back envelopes are not readily available. 15 Together, these findings suggest opportunities to improve counseling, storage, and disposal practices and reduce the amount of unused opioids remaining after treatment for acute pain.

text.text: Counseling on the importance of opioid disposal and appropriate disposal methods was uncommon, with similar rates observed across clinical settings and pain sources.

Among participants who received counseling, pharmacists were more commonly reported as the sole source of counseling than prescribers, highlighting the important role of pharmacists while also suggesting missed opportunities to reinforce counseling throughout the medication-use process.

This finding is particularly relevant given current recommendations that prescribers and pharmacists counsel patients on secure storage and safe disposal of unused opioids. 1, 19, 20 Previous studies have similarly found that counseling on safe opioid storage and disposal is not consistently provided to patients prescribed opioids. 21, 22 The similar counseling rates observed across clinical settings in our study, despite differences in clinical workflow and the amount and allocation of clinician-patient time across these settings, [23] [24] [25] suggest that limited counseling may reflect a broader gap in counseling practices when opioids are prescribed for acute pain, rather than being concentrated within settings where opportunities for patient counseling may be more limited.

text.text: Most participants with available storage responses did not consistently store opioids in a secure location, with three-quarters of them reporting that they never stored their opioids in a locked location.

Previous studies have similarly found that unused opioids are frequently stored in unsecured locations after treatment for acute pain, with systematic reviews reporting that approximately 70% or more of patients with leftover opioids did not store them in a locked location. 11, 26 Participants with children in the household in our study were more likely to store opioids in a latched or locked location than those without children, suggesting that concerns about children may influence storage practices.

text.text: However, the risks of unsecured storage extend beyond children and include other family members and friends, who may access opioids kept in the home, including medications taken without asking. 7, 27 The presence of children was not associated with whether participants kept leftover opioids, suggesting that greater attention to secure storage may not necessarily translate into removing unused opioids from the home.

text.text: These findings highlight the importance of counseling about both secure storage and disposal of unused opioids, regardless of whether children are present in the household.

Approximately two-thirds of participants who responded to questions on opioid leftovers and disposition did not use all of the opioids prescribed to them, and among those with leftover opioids, more than 40% kept them instead of disposing of them.

Previous studies have similarly found that patients often keep unused opioids for possible future pain, suggesting that leftover medications may be viewed as useful for subsequent episodes of pain. 28, 29 In our study, having medication available for future use, either for the same condition or a different condition, was the most commonly reported reason for keeping leftover opioids, while not knowing how to properly dispose of them was reported much less frequently.

text.text: This difference is important because providing instructions on how to dispose of unused opioids alone may have limited effects on reducing the amount of medication patients keep.
Counseling may also need to address the potential risks of keeping and using leftover opioids for future episodes of pain without a new clinical assessment.
In addition, prescribing quantities that more closely reflect patients' expected needs may reduce the amount of unused opioids remaining after treatment for acute pain.
This study has several limitations.
First, not all participants completed each follow-up survey or responded to each question, resulting in variation in the availability of data across study outcomes.

In particular, information on opioid leftovers and disposition was available for approximately half of participants, and there were minor but statistically significant differences in observed characteristics between respondents and non-respondents, which may introduce selection bias.
Second, counseling, instructions on opioid use, storage, opioid leftovers, and disposal practices were based on participant selfreport and may be subject to recall or social desirability bias.

Third, although we assessed whether participants reported receiving counseling on the importance of opioid disposal and appropriate disposal methods, we had limited information on the specific content, duration, or quality of that counseling beyond the disposal methods recommended.

We therefore could not determine whether the counseling provided differed across clinical settings or whether differences in counseling content or quality were associated with subsequent opioid storage or disposal practices.

Fourth, this analysis was conducted as part of the APP study, which was not specifically designed or powered to detect differences in opioid counseling, storage, and disposal outcomes across participant groups.
Therefore, the analyses were exploratory.

In addition, although we adjusted for several demographic and clinical characteristics, differences in patient populations across clinical settings, particularly the limited overlap in pain sources between dental practices and other settings, may have resulted in residual confounding and influenced the observed associations.
We also did not adjust for the quantity of opioids prescribed, which may have influenced storage practices and leftover opioids.

Lastly, although participants were recruited from multiple clinical settings and represented a range of acute pain conditions, all were opioid-naïve, which may limit the generalizability of these findings outside that population.

In this multicenter prospective cohort study of opioid-naïve patients prescribed opioids for acute pain, we found that counseling about opioid disposal was uncommon, secure storage was infrequent, and leftover opioids were frequent, with many patients keeping unused opioids for possible future use.
These findings suggest opportunities to improve counseling on secure opioid storage and disposal, including addressing the potential risks of keeping leftover opioids.
